creative.title: Why did they stop teaching this in school?
creative.description:
Why Magnets Vanished from Medicine 🧲

Most people think a magnetic ring is a folk remedy.

Something your nan swore by.

Something with no real thinking behind it.

But the idea is far older than you’d guess.

For more than 2,000 years, Chinese healers pressed specific points on the fingers to ease aching joints.

They called it acupressure.

And in Victorian Britain, magnetic bands and belts for rheumatism sold by the thousand.

Chemists stocked them.

Families swore by them.

People wore them every day. 🔶

The thinking behind it was simple. 🧬

Your fingers are packed with nerve endings.

Ache travels to the brain along slow nerve paths.

Gentle, steady pressure travels along faster ones.

Give the fast signal something to carry, and the ache has to wait in the queue.

That’s why you rub a knuckle without thinking when it throbs.

The ring just never lets go. ⚡️

So why did it disappear?

The answer is exactly what you’d expect.

In 1899, aspirin arrived.

In the 1960s, ibuprofen was developed right here in Nottingham.

Medicine moved to whatever could be patented, packaged and prescribed.

You can’t patent a pressure point.

You can’t patent a magnet.

So nobody championed them.

Not banned.

Just left behind.

Forgotten. 👀

But not entirely.

Because one woman went looking for it again.

Her name is Rosie.

She watched her mum give up her knitting, then her baking, then sit in a jeweller’s while they cut off her wedding ring because her knuckles had swollen past it.

The doctor’s answer was “wear and tear, keep taking the ibuprofen.”

So she tried the rings.

The cheap ones snapped over swollen knuckles.

The magnets were glued in and washed down the sink.

The copper turned her mum’s finger green.

So she had one made properly.

Surgical steel that never stains.

Magnets sealed in, not glued.

An open side that slides on past a swollen knuckle instead of getting stuck on it.

She didn’t set out to start a company.

She just wanted her mum’s hands back.

If you’re interested, link’s below. 🔶

https://tryevercalm.co.uk/pages/evercalm-joint-pain

creative.title: Read this if you wake up stiff and achy
creative.description:
Three days after I retired, my daughter-in-law rang to drop her three kids on me. "You don't do anything anymore, Jan. You can have them." I smiled, said no, and spent the autumn teaching her exactly what "doing nothing" looks like.

I taught Year 2 at St Mary's Primary for 34 years. On my last day the children lined the corridor and clapped me out through the front doors, and I cried the whole way to my car.

That afternoon the staff gave me a leaving present. A walking stick, the posh kind people take up mountains, with three words burned into the handle.

Now go, Jan.

I put it in the umbrella stand by my front door. Remember that it's there.

Three days later I was at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and a library book when my phone lit up with my daughter-in-law's name.

In twelve years of being married to my son, Chloe has never once called me Mum. She calls me Jan, and she only ever rings when she needs something.

She didn't say hello.

"Jan, work's doing a team week in Marbella over October half-term. I'm not dragging three kids round a hotel, so I'll drop them at yours on the Saturday. For the week."

Then, before I could answer:

"You don't do anything anymore. You can have them."

I told her I'd have to think about it, because I'd been thinking about doing some things of my own.

She laughed. Not a nasty laugh, exactly. Worse. The kind of laugh you'd give a child who says she's going to be an astronaut.

"Things? Jan. You couldn't get round Disneyland with us. You sat on a bench all afternoon minding everybody's bags."

I said I'd help her find a childminder. She said childminders cost money.

So I smiled, which she couldn't see, and I said, I'm sorry, Chloe, I'll be busy that week. And I hung up.

I had never hung up on anyone in my life.

I need to tell you about that bench.

Two summers ago we all went to Disneyland Paris. My son Mark, Chloe, the three grandchildren and me. I paid for everybody's park tickets as my birthday present to the family.

By eleven o'clock on the first morning my knees were done. My back had locked, my feet were on fire, and I was so tired I could have lain down on the cobbles. So I found a bench near the castle and told everybody to go on without me.

I sat on that bench for five hours. Buggies, rucksacks, a changing bag and everybody's water bottles piled up around me like I was the cloakroom.

My grandchildren went on everything. I have one photo from that whole trip, and I'm holding a crêpe and a changing bag.

An hour after I hung up on Chloe, my phone started buzzing with the family WhatsApp. Twenty-three people. My son, my sister, the cousins, half the family I've cooked Christmas dinner for since 1991.

Chloe had posted a picture of the hotel. Palm trees, blue pools. "Team week 🌺 Mark's got the kids. Some of us still work."

Then a second picture.

It was me, on that bench in Paris. Shoes off, mouth open, fast asleep, with a buggy and four rucksacks piled up around me.

Underneath it she'd written: "Nana's got PLANS 😂"

Three people laughed at it.

My son hearted it.

I'm not proud of what I did next. I went into my account and changed the Netflix password she'd been using for six years.

It felt wonderful for about four minutes.

Then I sat at my kitchen table and looked at that photo for a long, long time. The woman asleep on the bench. Her shoes off. Everybody's bags piled round her like she was part of the furniture.

Because the part I'd never said out loud was that Chloe wasn't wrong.

I'm 63, and somewhere in the last few years I'd slowed down so much I barely recognised myself. I woke up every morning crippled, crumpled and generally knackered. I was stiff the second I swung my legs out of bed. I went up the stairs dragging myself on the handrail. My long walks had turned into ten-minute walks, and then into no walks, because I couldn't get round my own estate without stopping.

I was wiped out by three in the afternoon and wide awake at three in the morning. When my grandson wanted me down on the floor with his Lego, I'd say not today, sweetheart, because I knew I'd need help getting back up.

I'd started doing the Tesco shop online so I didn't have to walk round the big one. I'd started saying "you lot go on ahead" so often that people stopped waiting.

And I was doing everything right. Glucosamine, turmeric, collagen, cod liver oil, vitamin D and magnesium. Paracetamol, ibuprofen and Voltarol that didn't touch the sides. Two blocks of physio. My GP gave me seven minutes. "It's wear and tear, Jan. Take paracetamol. See you in twenty years."

So maybe Chloe had it right. Maybe this was who I was now. The woman who doesn't do anything anymore.

Then I looked over at the umbrella stand by the door.

Now go, Jan.

I opened Chloe's photo of the hotel again. She'd tagged it.

I booked a room for the same week.

Then I sat back in my chair and my hands started shaking, because I'd just booked a week in Marbella, twelve weeks away, and I couldn't get round a theme park without a bench.

That Sunday was Dot Pickering's 79th birthday party. Dot ran the school office at St Mary's for 31 years before I ever got there, and she still knows every child's name and every teacher's secret.

I almost didn't go. I'm glad I did.

Dot wasn't sitting down at her own party. She was carrying a plate of sausage rolls round the garden. Then she was down on the lawn with her great-grandchildren, looking for a ball under the hedge. Then she was back up again, without putting a hand on anything, and I watched her do it like I was watching a magic trick.

She's sixteen years older than me. If I'd gone down on that lawn, somebody would have had to winch me back up.

So when she finally sat down next to me, I asked her straight out. Dot, how on earth are you doing that at 79?

She laughed so hard she had to put her plate down.

"Love, at 70 I couldn't get off my own settee without rocking three times. My daughter was pricing up stairlifts. I was about this close to letting her."

Then she held up her right hand. A slim gold ring, worn soft at the edges.

"My sister put this on me. She's 84 and still drives herself to Cornwall every Easter. I wore it to shut her up."

I told her I'd confiscated better jewellery than that from seven-year-olds.

"So did I," she said. "So I took it off for a week to prove her wrong. By Thursday I was back on that settee, rocking."

Then she explained it the way Dot explains everything, like you're a supply teacher about to be late for registration.

"Your blood runs through little tubes, Jan. When you're young they're soft and stretchy. After fifty they stiffen up, like an old garden hose left out all winter. So the blood slows down, and everything it feeds goes stiff and heavy and tired."

"You remember the master clock in my office? The one that rang every bell in the building? When that clock ran slow, the whole school went haywire. Kids late for dinner, playtime running over, coaches sat in the car park, and every teacher in the building blaming every other teacher. It was never the teachers. It was one clock."

"Your knees, your back, your sleep, the three o'clock slump. You don't have five problems, love. You've got one clock running slow."

I thought about my kitchen cupboard. All those bottles. Every one of them for a different teacher.

"And this," she said, tapping her hand, "is the office."

She took my hand and pressed the back of my finger, just below the knuckle. "Healers have been pressing points on the fingers for thousands of years to ease pain somewhere else entirely. There's four little magnets on the inside of this ring, sat right on those points. They send a pulse into the blood vessels, all day and all night. Softens them up. Gets the blood moving. Puts the clock back on time."

I asked why I couldn't just press it myself.

"You'd have to sit there pressing it all day. This does it while you're asleep."

Then why had no doctor ever said a single word about it?

"Seven minutes, Jan. They haven't got time to tell you about your own blood."

And then the question I was actually scared to ask. Is this going to get me through a week in Marbella?

"No," she said. "Your legs are. This just gets the blood back to them."

I already had my phone out, looking at the £9.99 ones on Amazon. She took it right out of my hand.

"Not those. Two weak magnets in a band that turns you green, and you take it off at bedtime. That's why everybody thinks it's a gimmick. Off is no good, Jan. The minute it's off, the clock slows down again."

Then she reached into her handbag, took out a pad of old St Mary's late slips that she apparently still carries, and wrote a name on the back of one.

EverCalm.

"Get the gold one. When's your trip?"

October half-term. Twelve weeks.

"Then order it tonight. And Jan? Don't you dare tell that girl you're coming."

I ordered it sat in Dot's drive.

Week 1. Nothing at all. I texted Dot that I wanted my late slip back.

Week 2. I slept through the night. I woke up at seven and checked the clock twice.

Week 3. I came down the stairs, put the kettle on, and I was pouring the milk before I noticed I hadn't touched the handrail.

Week 5. I took it off to prove Dot wrong, the same way she had. By day four I was stiff again and back on the settee by three. I put it back on, and it hasn't left my finger since.

Week 6. Three o'clock came and went, and I didn't sit down. I didn't even notice until tea.

Week 7. I got down on the floor with my grandson's Lego, and I got back up by myself.

Week 8. I took the walking stick out of the umbrella stand and walked the three-mile loop round the reservoir. The next morning, I did it again.

Week 10. My sister met me for lunch and stopped dead in the doorway of the café. "Janet. What are you taking?"

Week 12. I packed my suitcase. My good jeans needed a belt. Half a stone.

The ring didn't walk that half stone off me. I did. It just gave me back a body that wanted to move.

That's what doing nothing looks like, by the way.

On the Saturday of half-term, I got a taxi to Manchester Airport by myself.

Chloe had no idea I was coming.

She found out at the hotel pool on the Sunday afternoon. She was walking past with two women from her office, and she stopped so fast one of them walked into the back of her.

"Jan? What are you doing here?"

Doing nothing, I said. Like you told me.

On the Tuesday the whole team went on a day trip up into the mountains. Nobody had invited me. I'd put my name down at reception the day I arrived, and I was the first one on the coach.

It was the Caminito del Rey. They used to call it the most dangerous path in the world. A narrow walkway bolted to the side of a gorge, a hundred metres of nothing underneath, and a swaying bridge at the very end.

At the start, the guide asked if anybody wanted to stay with the coach and mind the bags.

I picked up my walking stick and set off.

Now go, Jan.

I was standing in the middle of that bridge when the group caught up. A young lad from Chloe's office came over with his hands on his knees, puffing.

"Sorry, I've got to ask. How old are you?"

63, I said.

"My mum's 58 and she can't do her own stairs. What are you on?"

Chloe was right behind him. She heard every word.

And when we got back to the start, there was one person sitting on the bench by the coach, minding everybody's bags.

Chloe. She'd turned her ankle on the stony path down to the start and come back to wait, with a bag of ice from the cool box on her foot.

I took one picture. Just one.

I've never posted it.

On the Friday night the hotel put on a flamenco night. When the dancers came round pulling people up, they pulled me, in front of Chloe's entire office, and I danced the whole song.

When I sat back down, a woman about my age leaned over from the next table.

"I'm sorry, I have to ask. I've watched you all week. What's your secret?"

I held up my hand. I told her about Dot and the late slip, and about the four little magnets and the clock.

Chloe was three seats down. She put her fork down and didn't pick it up again.

That night she knocked on my door.

No make-up. Hair in a clip. Her ankle wrapped in a tea towel full of ice from the bar.

She sat down in the other chair on my balcony, and for a long time she didn't say anything.

"I put that picture on the family WhatsApp," she said finally.

You did.

"I've been telling everyone for two years that you can't keep up. That you just sit." She looked at her ankle. "And this week I'm the one who sat on a bench minding everybody's bags."

I let that sit.

"Everybody always talks about how you brought Mark up on your own. How you did everything. I've got three kids and a full-time job and I'm drowning, Jan. It was easier if you were the one who couldn't."

"I said you don't do anything anymore. That was a horrible thing to say."

It was the first thing she'd ever said to me that didn't have a smile on top of it.

Then she looked at my hand.

"Where do I get one? Not for me. For my mum. She's 61, and I haven't invited her anywhere in three years because I thought she'd slow us down."

I told her to leave her mother to me.

And then I told her something I hadn't planned to say. If she ever needed me to have the kids for a weekend, I would. Not because I don't do anything anymore. Because I want to.

She cried. A proper cry, the first I'd ever seen from her.

I changed the Netflix password back the next morning.

My son rang that afternoon. She'd told him everything.

"Mum. That picture. I'm so sorry. I should have said something years ago."

I know, love.

Chloe rang me again last week, to ask what time she should drop the kids off. Right before she hung up, she said, "Thanks, Mum."

Twelve years. First time.

Somewhere over the Bay of Biscay on the way home, I worked out what that autumn had really been about.

For 34 years I looked after everybody. Then my body slowed down, and the people I'd looked after decided I was the one who needed looking after.

And the worst part is, I half believed them.

I wasn't old. My clock was running slow, and in 63 years nobody had ever told me why.

When I got home I went back on the EverCalm site and ordered twice more, because while the offer's on, every ring you buy comes with a second one free.

1 for my sister.

1 for the woman at the flamenco night, who wrote her email on a paper napkin.

1 for the lad from the gorge, for his mum who can't do her stairs.

And 1 for Chloe's mum. Chloe drove it round to her herself.

You get 30 days, and if you feel nothing, you send it back for every penny. My first week did nothing, so don't judge yours on the first week. Give it the month.

Maybe nobody has called you free childcare.

But maybe you've become the one who minds the bags. Maybe your long walks have turned into short ones, and then into none. Maybe someone has decided you don't do anything anymore, and the worst part is that you've started to agree with them.

It may not be your age. It may be one clock, running slow, that nobody has ever bothered to check.

I didn't go to Marbella to embarrass her. I iced her ankle, and I'm having her kids next month.

I went because I'd spent five hours asleep on a bench at Disneyland, and I wasn't going to spend the rest of my life on it.

Somebody has already decided you're the one who minds the bags.

Put them down, and go.

Why Magnets Vanished from Medicine 🧲

Most people think a magnetic ring is a folk remedy.

Something your nan swore by.

Something with no real thinking behind it.

But the idea is far older than you’d guess.

For more than 2,000 years, Chinese healers pressed specific points on the fingers to ease aching joints.

They called it acupressure.

And in Victorian Britain, magnetic bands and belts for rheumatism sold by the thousand.

Chemists stocked them.

Families swore by them.

People wore them every day. 🔶

The thinking behind it was simple. 🧬

Your fingers are packed with nerve endings.

Ache travels to the brain along slow nerve paths.

Gentle, steady pressure travels along faster ones.

Give the fast signal something to carry, and the ache has to wait in the queue.

That’s why you rub a knuckle without thinking when it throbs.

The ring just never lets go. ⚡️

So why did it disappear?

The answer is exactly what you’d expect.

In 1899, aspirin arrived.

In the 1960s, ibuprofen was developed right here in Nottingham.

Medicine moved to whatever could be patented, packaged and prescribed.

You can’t patent a pressure point.

You can’t patent a magnet.

So nobody championed them.

Not banned.

Just left behind.

Forgotten. 👀

But not entirely.

Because one woman went looking for it again.

Her name is Rosie.

She watched her mum give up her knitting, then her baking, then sit in a jeweller’s while they cut off her wedding ring because her knuckles had swollen past it.

The doctor’s answer was “wear and tear, keep taking the ibuprofen.”

So she tried the rings.

The cheap ones snapped over swollen knuckles.

The magnets were glued in and washed down the sink.

The copper turned her mum’s finger green.

So she had one made properly.

Surgical steel that never stains.

Magnets sealed in, not glued.

An open side that slides on past a swollen knuckle instead of getting stuck on it.

She didn’t set out to start a company.

She just wanted her mum’s hands back.

creative.description:
At my daughter's engagement party, my ex-husband's new wife told me she'd be doing my dance with my daughter. "You can't really dance anymore, Linda. You can just watch." I smiled, said fine, and spent the next twelve weeks teaching her exactly what "just watch" looks like.

I was a dinner lady at St Mary's Primary for 22 years. I brought Emma up mostly on my own after Steve left. Every Saturday morning when she was little, we danced round the kitchen to "Dancing Queen" in our pyjamas. When she was six she made me promise we'd dance to it at her wedding.

When the divorce came through eight years ago, my sister bought me a pair of red dancing shoes. Proper ones, with a little heel. On the inside of the box lid she'd written three words in lipstick.

Now go, Linda.

I put them at the bottom of my wardrobe. Remember that they're there.

Emma's engagement party was at Steve's house, because Steve's house has a garden room and a hot tub. Tasha met me at the door with a glass of prosecco and an iPad.

In eight years of being married to my ex-husband, Tasha has never once said my name without "bless her" on the end of it. She's 41, she teaches Pilates, and she talks about it more than she does it.

She didn't say hello.

""Linda, quick one. Emma and I were talking about the mother-and-daughter dance. I think it makes more sense if I do it with her."

Then, before I could answer:

"You can't really dance anymore, can you? You can just watch, bless her."

Emma looked at her shoes. I told Tasha that Emma and I had been doing that dance since she was six.

She laughed. Not a nasty laugh, exactly. Worse. The kind of laugh you'd give a child who says she's going to be an astronaut.

"The dance floor? Linda. You couldn't get through cousin Becky's wedding. You sat at the handbag table all night."

Emma said, "Mum, she's only thinking of your knees." Tasha said that was all she was doing.

So I smiled, and I said, Fine, Tasha. And I took my prosecco out to the garden.

I had never walked away from anyone mid-sentence in my life.

I need to tell you about that table.

Two summers ago we all went to my niece Becky's wedding at a hotel outside Chester. Emma, Steve, Tasha, my sister and me. I'd bought a new dress and had my hair done in town.

By the speeches my knees were done. My back had locked, my feet were on fire, and I was so tired I could have lain down on the carpet. So when the band started, I stayed at the table by the dance floor and told everybody to go on without me.

I sat at that table for five hours. Eleven handbags, a pile of jackets, a box of favours and everybody's drinks piled up around me like I was the cloakroom.

Everybody danced to everything. I have one photo from that whole night, and I'm holding a slice of cake and somebody else's clutch bag.

An hour after the engagement party, my phone started buzzing with the wedding WhatsApp. "Emma & Josh 💍". Twenty-three people. Emma, Steve, my sister, the bridesmaids, half the family I've done Christmas for since 1991.

Tasha had posted a picture of the venue. A country house in the Cotswolds, and a long flight of stone steps down through the garden to the lake. "84 steps down to the ceremony 😍 Get your dancing shoes ready!"

Then a second picture.

It was me, at Becky's wedding. Shoes off, mouth open, fast asleep in my chair, with eleven handbags piled up around me.

Underneath it she'd written: "Linda's got the handbags covered 😂"

Three people laughed at it.

Steve hearted it.

I'm not proud of what I did next. The Netflix account Steve and Tasha had been using for eight years was still on my bank card. I went in and changed the password.

It felt wonderful for about four minutes.

Then I sat at my kitchen table and looked at that photo for a long, long time. The woman asleep at the table. Her shoes off. Everybody's handbags piled round her like she was part of the furniture.

Because the part I'd never said out loud was that Tasha wasn't wrong.

I'm 58, and somewhere in the last few years I'd slowed down so much I barely recognised myself. I woke up every morning crippled, crumpled and generally knackered. I went up the stairs dragging myself on the handrail. My long walks with the dog had turned into ten-minute walks, and then my neighbour's lad started taking him.

I was wiped out by three in the afternoon and wide awake at three in the morning. When the dog's ball went under the settee, I'd leave it there, because I knew I'd need the settee to get back up.

I'd started doing the Tesco shop online so I didn't have to walk round the big one. I'd started saying "you lot go on ahead" so often that people stopped waiting.

And I was doing everything right. Glucosamine, turmeric, collagen, cod liver oil, vitamin D and magnesium. Paracetamol, ibuprofen and Voltarol that didn't touch the sides. Two blocks of physio. My GP gave me seven minutes. "It's wear and tear, Linda. Take paracetamol. See you in twenty years."

So maybe Tasha had it right. Maybe this was who I was now. The woman who just watches.

Then I thought about the bottom of my wardrobe.

Now go, Linda.

I opened my emails and wrote to the wedding band. One song, one line.

"Dancing Queen". For the mother of the bride.

Then I sat back in my chair and my hands started shaking, because my only daughter was getting married in twelve weeks at the bottom of 84 stone steps, and I couldn't get through a wedding without the handbag table.

That Sunday was Dot Pickering's 79th birthday party. Dot ran the school office at St Mary's for 31 years. She knows every child's name, every dinner lady's secret, and exactly how many fish fingers I served between 1998 and 2020.

I almost didn't go. I'm glad I did.

Dot wasn't sitting down at her own party. She was carrying a plate of sausage rolls round the garden. Then she was down on the lawn with her great-grandchildren, looking for a ball under the hedge. Then she was back up again, without putting a hand on anything, and I watched her do it like I was watching a magic trick.

She's 21 years older than me. If I'd gone down on that lawn, somebody would have had to winch me back up.

So when she finally sat down next to me, I asked her straight out. Dot, how on earth are you doing that at 79?

She laughed so hard she had to put her plate down.

"Love, at 70 I couldn't get off my own settee without rocking three times. My daughter was pricing up stairlifts. I was about this close to letting her."

Then she held up her right hand. A slim gold ring, worn soft at the edges.

"My sister put this on me. She's 84 and still drives herself to Cornwall every Easter. I wore it to shut her up."

I told her I'd seen better rings in a Christmas cracker.

"So did I," she said. "So I took it off for a week to prove her wrong. By Thursday I was back on that settee, rocking."

Then she explained it the way Dot explains everything, like you're a supply teacher about to be late for registration.

"Your blood runs through little tubes, Linda. When you're young they're soft and stretchy. After fifty they stiffen up, like an old garden hose left out all winter. So the blood slows down, and everything it feeds goes stiff and heavy and tired."

"You remember the master clock in my office? The one that rang every bell in the building? When that clock ran slow, the whole school went haywire. Kids late for dinner, playtime running over, coaches sat in the car park, and every teacher in the building blaming every other teacher. It was never the teachers. It was one clock."

"Your knees, your back, your sleep, the three o'clock slump. You don't have five problems, love. You've got one clock running slow."

I thought about my kitchen cupboard. All those bottles. Every one of them for a different teacher.

"And this," she said, tapping her hand, "is the office."

She took my hand and pressed the back of my finger, just below the knuckle. "Healers have been pressing points on the fingers for thousands of years to ease pain somewhere else entirely. There's four little magnets on the inside of this ring, sat right on those points. They send a pulse into the blood vessels, all day and all night. Softens them up. Gets the blood moving. Puts the clock back on time."

I asked why I couldn't just press it myself.

"You'd have to sit there pressing it all day. This does it while you're asleep."

Then why had no doctor ever said a single word about it?

"Seven minutes, Linda. They haven't got time to tell you about your own blood."

And then the question I was actually scared to ask. Is this going to get me down 84 steps and onto that dance floor with my daughter?

"No," she said. "Your legs are. This just gets the blood back to them."

I already had my phone out, looking at the £9.99 ones on Amazon. She took it right out of my hand.

"Not those. Two weak magnets in a band that turns you green, and you take it off at bedtime. That's why everybody thinks it's a gimmick. Off is no good, Linda. The minute it's off, the clock slows down again."

Then she reached into her handbag, took out a pad of old St Mary's late slips that she apparently still carries, and wrote a name on the back of one.

EverCalm.

"Get the gold one. It'll go with your dress. When's the wedding?"

Twelve weeks on Saturday.

"Then order it tonight. And Linda? Don't you dare tell that woman you're dancing."

I ordered it sat in Dot's drive.

Week 1. Nothing at all. I texted Dot that I wanted my late slip back.

Week 2. I slept through the night. I woke up at seven and checked the clock twice.

Week 3. I came down the stairs, put the kettle on, and I was pouring the milk before I noticed I hadn't touched the handrail.

Week 5. I took it off to prove Dot wrong, the same way she had. By day four I was stiff again and back on the settee by three. I put it back on, and it hasn't left my finger since.

Week 6. Three o'clock came and went, and I didn't sit down. I didn't even notice until tea.

Week 7. The dog's ball went under the settee. I got down, got it, and got back up by myself. He looked as surprised as I was.

Week 8. I took the red shoes out of the bottom of the wardrobe and danced round the kitchen to "Dancing Queen". Then I walked the three-mile loop round the reservoir. The next morning, I did both again.

Week 10. My sister came with me for the dress fitting and stopped dead in the doorway of the shop. "Lin. What are you taking?"

Week 12. The dress needed taking in. Half a stone.

The ring didn't walk that half stone off me. I did. It just gave me back a body that wanted to move.

That's what "just watch" looks like, by the way.

On the morning of the wedding, I drove myself down to the Cotswolds in the red shoes.

Tasha had no idea what was coming.

She found out at the top of the steps. She was on Steve's arm in a pair of five-inch heels, holding the handrail with both hands. The wedding coordinator was telling the older guests there was a golf buggy round the side, for anyone who'd rather not do the steps.

Tasha looked at me and nodded at the buggy.

I took my sister's arm, and then I let go of it.

Now go, Linda.

Eighty-four steps. I counted every one. I was in my seat by the lake, second row, before Steve and Tasha were halfway down.

Josh's best man sat down behind me, a bit out of breath. "Sorry, I've got to ask. How old are you?"

58, I said.

"My mum's 55 and she can't do her own stairs. What are you on?"

Tasha was right behind him. She heard every word.

She turned her ankle on step 61. Her heel caught in a gap in the stone. The golf buggy came round and took her back up to the house, and she watched my daughter get married from the terrace with a bag of ice on her foot.

At the reception, she spent the whole night at the table by the dance floor, with her foot on a chair and everybody's handbags piled round her.

I took one picture. Just one.

I've never posted it.

When it came to the mother-and-daughter dance, the band leader looked over at Tasha. Tasha looked at her ankle.

Then the first notes of "Dancing Queen" started, and Emma came and found me. "You emailed them, didn't you, Mum?" She pulled me onto the dance floor in front of 140 people, and we danced the whole song, the way we did in the kitchen when she was six. And the next one. And the conga at midnight.

When I finally sat down, Josh's auntie leaned over from the next table.

"I'm sorry, I have to ask. I've watched you all day. What's your secret?"

I held up my hand. I told her about Dot and the late slip, and about the four little magnets and the clock.

Tasha was at the table by the dance floor, with her foot up on a chair. She put her glass down and didn't pick it up again.

Half an hour later, she found me in the ladies.

Mascara gone. Hair coming down. Her ankle wrapped in a napkin full of ice from the bar.

She leaned on the sink next to me, and for a long time she didn't say anything.

"I put that picture on the WhatsApp," she said finally.

You did.

"I've been telling everyone for eight years that you can't keep up. That you just sit." She looked down at her ankle. "And today I'm the one who sat at the table minding everybody's handbags."

I let that sit.

"Steve talks about you all the time. How you brought Emma up on your own. How you did everything. I've got a stepdaughter who's never going to like me, and a husband who still calls me Linda by mistake. It was easier if you were the one who couldn't."

"I tried to take your dance. That was a horrible thing to do."

It was the first thing she'd ever said to me that didn't have a smile on top of it.

Then she looked at my hand.

"Where do I get one? Not for me. For my mum. She's 66, and I haven't taken her anywhere in three years because I thought she'd slow me down."

I told her to leave her mother to me.

And then I told her something I hadn't planned to say. If she ever wanted to come to Sunday dinner at Emma's, she should. Not because she has to. Because Emma would like it, and so would I.

She cried. A proper cry, the first I'd ever seen from her. At the door she turned round and said, "Thanks, Linda."

No "bless her". Eight years. First time.

I changed the Netflix password back the next morning.

Steve rang that afternoon. "Lin. That picture. I'm sorry. I should have said something years ago."

I know, Steve.

A week later Emma posted the photographer's pictures on the WhatsApp. The first one was me in the middle of the conga in my red shoes, with my head thrown back, laughing.

Underneath she'd written: "Mum's got PLANS 😂"

Twenty-three people hearted it. Tasha was the first.

Somewhere on the M5 on the way home, I'd worked out what those twelve weeks had really been about.

For 30 years I looked after everybody. Then my body slowed down, and the people I'd looked after decided I was the one who should just watch.

And the worst part is, I half believed them.

I wasn't old. My clock was running slow, and in 58 years nobody had ever told me why.

When I got home I went back on the EverCalm site and ordered twice more, because while the offer's on, every ring you buy comes with a second one free.

1 for my sister.

1 for Josh's auntie, who wrote her email on the back of a place card.

1 for the best man, for his mum who can't do her stairs.

And 1 for Tasha's mum. Tasha drove it round to her herself.

You get 30 days, and if you feel nothing, you send it back for every penny. My first week did nothing, so don't judge yours on the first week. Give it the month.

Maybe nobody has tried to take your dance.

But maybe you've become the one who minds the handbags. Maybe your long walks have turned into short ones, and then into none. Maybe someone has decided you should just watch, and the worst part is that you've started to agree with them.

It may not be your age. It may be one clock, running slow, that nobody has ever bothered to check.

I didn't dance at my daughter's wedding to embarrass Tasha. I iced her ankle, and she's coming to Sunday dinner next week.

I danced because I'd spent five hours asleep at a handbag table at Becky's wedding, and I wasn't going to spend the rest of my life at one.

Somebody has already decided you're the one who minds the handbags.

Put them down, and dance.

Doing nothing, I said. Like you told me.

On the Tuesday the whole team went on a day trip up into the mountains. Nobody had invited me. I'd put my name down at reception the day I arrived, and I was the first one on the coach.

It was the Caminito del Rey. They used to call it the most dangerous path in the world. A narrow walkway bolted to the side of a gorge, a hundred metres of nothing underneath, and a swaying bridge at the very end.

At the start, the guide asked if anybody wanted to stay with the coach and mind the bags.

I picked up my walking stick and set off.

Now go, Jan.

I was standing in the middle of that bridge when the group caught up. A young lad from Chloe's office came over with his hands on his knees, puffing.

"Sorry, I've got to ask. How old are you?"

63, I said.

"My mum's 58 and she can't do her own stairs. What are you on?"

Chloe was right behind him. She heard every word.

And when we got back to the start, there was one person sitting on the bench by the coach, minding everybody's bags.

Chloe. She'd turned her ankle on the stony path down to the start and come back to wait, with a bag of ice from the cool box on her foot.

I took one picture. Just one.

I've never posted it.

On the Friday night the hotel put on a flamenco night. When the dancers came round pulling people up, they pulled me, in front of Chloe's entire office, and I danced the whole song.

When I sat back down, a woman about my age leaned over from the next table.

"I'm sorry, I have to ask. I've watched you all week. What's your secret?"

I held up my hand. I told her about Dot and the late slip, and about the four little magnets and the clock.

Chloe was three seats down. She put her fork down and didn't pick it up again.

That night she knocked on my door.

No make-up. Hair in a clip. Her ankle wrapped in a tea towel full of ice from the bar.

She sat down in the other chair on my balcony, and for a long time she didn't say anything.

"I put that picture on the family WhatsApp," she said finally.

You did.

"I've been telling everyone for two years that you can't keep up. That you just sit." She looked at her ankle. "And this week I'm the one who sat on a bench minding everybody's bags."

I let that sit.

"Everybody always talks about how you brought Mark up on your own. How you did everything. I've got three kids and a full-time job and I'm drowning, Jan. It was easier if you were the one who couldn't."

"I said you don't do anything anymore. That was a horrible thing to say."

It was the first thing she'd ever said to me that didn't have a smile on top of it.

Then she looked at my hand.

"Where do I get one? Not for me. For my mum. She's 61, and I haven't invited her anywhere in three years because I thought she'd slow us down."

I told her to leave her mother to me.

And then I told her something I hadn't planned to say. If she ever needed me to have the kids for a weekend, I would. Not because I don't do anything anymore. Because I want to.

She cried. A proper cry, the first I'd ever seen from her.

I changed the Netflix password back the next morning.

My son rang that afternoon. She'd told him everything.

"Mum. That picture. I'm so sorry. I should have said something years ago."

I know, love.

Chloe rang me again last week, to ask what time she should drop the kids off. Right before she hung up, she said, "Thanks, Mum."

Twelve years. First time.

For 34 years I looked after everybody. Then my body slowed down, and the people I'd looked after decided I was the one who needed looking after.
